title: The CSAT Drop

scenario.situation: Average CSAT fell from 4.4 to 3.9 this month across all support tickets.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The Support Director is convinced agents have gotten sloppy — she wants to launch a coaching plan and flag low-scorers in their performance reviews.
scenario.question: Is the CSAT drop actually an agent-quality problem?

decisions.prompt: The Support Director wants action now. How do you frame the investigation before touching the agent data?

options.label: Rank agents by CSAT and find the low performers
options.detail: Pull each agent's average CSAT this month vs. last and sort ascending to find who dropped.
options.consequence: You produce a ranking — but if the overall metric is broken, the ranking inherits the same flaw. You've identified which agents are lowest in a corrupted sample, not who actually declined in quality.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the Director's hypothesis and inherited the metric's hidden flaw.

options.label: Audit the metric itself before blaming the people it measures
options.detail: Ask: did anything change about HOW or WHOM CSAT is collected from before asking whether agents changed?
options.consequence: You surface two recent changes — a new survey trigger and a ticket-mix shift toward billing issues — that could move the number without any agent behavior changing. This is the thread.

options.label: Run a regression of CSAT on agent attributes
options.detail: Model CSAT as a function of agent tenure, shift, and ticket volume to find structural causes.
options.consequence: The model returns some significant coefficients, but you're fitting a noisy, potentially biased outcome variable. Sophistication here amplifies the measurement problem rather than diagnosing it.
options.divergenceCost: Jumped to modeling before validating the outcome metric — garbage in, garbage out.

options.label: Survey customers who gave low scores
options.detail: Follow up with 1-star and 2-star raters to ask what went wrong.
options.consequence: Qualitative feedback trickles in slowly and reflects the already-skewed responder pool. You get color on why angry customers are angry, but no signal on whether agent quality actually changed.
options.divergenceCost: Chose a slow instrument that samples from the same biased pool causing the problem.

decisions.prompt: You find that a new survey trigger launched this month AND billing tickets spiked. Which cut of the data do you trust to assess agent quality?

artifact.title: Average CSAT by ticket category — this month (all respondents)
artifact.caption: Raw CSAT averages by category this month. Billing drags the overall score — but is that agents, or the broken billing feature itself?

options.label: Overall average CSAT, month-over-month
options.detail: Compare this month's 3.9 to last month's 4.4 across all tickets and all respondents.
options.consequence: The 0.5-point drop looks damning, but it folds together a response-pool change (angrier customers now get the survey) and a ticket-mix shift (more billing tickets). You cannot tell if agents caused any of it.
options.divergenceCost: Used an aggregate that conflates measurement change, mix shift, and agent quality into one uninterpretable number.

options.label: Agent CSAT on non-billing tickets, like-for-like responder cohort
options.detail: Hold ticket category constant (exclude billing) and compare only customers who met the OLD trigger criteria both months.
options.consequence: Controlling for category and responder eligibility, agent CSAT on comparable tickets is 4.3 this month vs. 4.4 last month — a 0.1-point difference well within normal variance. Agent quality is essentially flat; the drop lives entirely in mix shift and sample composition.

artifact.title: Agent CSAT — non-billing tickets, like-for-like responder cohort

bars.label: This month (billing excluded, old trigger criteria)

artifact.caption: When you hold the measurement population and ticket mix constant, agent performance is unchanged. The drop is entirely explained by who is surveyed and what they needed help with.

decisions.prompt: Like-for-like data shows agents are flat, but billing tickets tanked CSAT. What do you tell the Support Director?

options.label: "It's 100% the billing bug and the survey trigger — agents are fine, cancel the coaching plan."
options.detail: Make the full causal claim and recommend no agent action.
options.consequence: You've correctly identified the drivers, but overclaiming certainty means the Director either dismisses you as defensive of agents, or acts on your word without a verifiable path. If any residual agent issue exists, it goes unmonitored.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed certainty and left no mechanism for the Director to verify or for real agent issues to surface.

options.label: "The metric moved because of who we're measuring and what they asked about — agent quality looks stable, but let's confirm with a clean scorecard before closing the loop."
options.detail: Present the mix-shift and responder-bias findings, hold the causal claim appropriately, and propose a like-for-like agent scorecard going forward.
options.consequence: The Director sees the evidence reframing her assumption, understands the measurement problem, and agrees to pause the coaching plan while a cleaner CSAT instrument is designed. You've protected agents from an unfair action and improved the measurement system.

insight: The CSAT drop was not an agent-quality story — it was a measurement story. A new survey trigger selectively captured dissatisfied customers, and a spike in billing tickets (driven by a broken feature) flooded the sample with low scores that had nothing to do with agent behavior. The lesson is that a metric's population can shift under you without anyone noticing: before blaming the people being measured, audit who is being measured, under what conditions, and whether the mix of what they experienced has changed.
